analysis.one_liner: Cuts the Pentagon budget by $100 billion and protects military health, pay, and civilian jobs from the cut.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut the Defense Department budget by $100 billion never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Armed Services Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set the Pentagon's authorized budget for fiscal 2024 at $100 billion below what was spent in fiscal 2023, and it directs the Defense Department to use a Congressional Budget Office study of a smaller defense budget to decide where the cuts fall. It shields three things from the cut: the Defense Health Program, military personnel accounts, and civilian employee pay and benefits. It also states Congress's view that many urgent national security threats are not military, and that the savings should be redirected to other national priorities.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, the money not spent on weapons programs and Pentagon operations would be available for other priorities, as the bill's sense-of-Congress section contemplates reallocation [S3]. Military families and Defense Department civilian employees would be protected from cuts, since the bill exempts health care, military pay, and civil service pay from the reductions [S2]. Taxpayers generally would benefit from a smaller defense budget.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, troops, and Defense civilian workers

how_it_helps.text: It cuts the amount authorized for the Department of Defense for fiscal 2024 by $100 billion below the fiscal 2023 level [S2].
It exempts the Defense Health Program, military personnel accounts, and civil service pay and benefits from the cuts, so health care and service members' pay are shielded [S2].
It states the sense of Congress that many urgent national security threats are not military and that savings should be reallocated to national priorities [S3].
It directs the Defense Secretary to use the CBO report 'Illustrative Options for National Defense Under a Smaller Defense Budget' to guide where reductions fall, rather than cutting blindly [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The defense industry and Pentagon program offices that would lose $100 billion in authorized funding, including contractors for weapons systems, operations, and research that would no longer be funded at current levels [S2]. Anyone who believes a larger military budget is needed for deterrence would bear the security risk the cut implies.

drawbacks.text: A $100 billion reduction, roughly ten percent or more of the defense budget, could reduce military readiness, procurement, and research, and critics would argue it weakens deterrence at a time of tensions with China and Russia [S2].

The bill only cuts the authorization; it does not actually redirect any money to specific domestic programs like health care, education, or housing, so the savings would depend on later spending decisions by Congress [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is that a defense budget larger than the next several countries' combined spends heavily on programs while other national needs go unmet, and the bill protects troops' pay and health care from the cut. The case against it is that a cut of this size would be abrupt and could hollow out military capacity, and that the bill does not guarantee any of the savings actually reach working people; it reduces Pentagon money without naming where it goes instead.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Armed Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it sat there until the Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Representative Barbara Lee introduced the bill on February 21, 2023, joined by 24 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Armed Services the same day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was taken: the full action history shows only the introduction and the referral, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Pentagon and its contractor base are better off, since the $100 billion cut never came to a vote and defense funding continued at authorized levels. House Armed Services Committee leadership is better off in the sense that its budget priorities were never tested on the floor.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the Pentagon budget by $100 billion and shield health and pay accounts.

for.name: 24 Democratic cosponsors (including Reps. Pocan, Jayapal, McGovern, Tlaib, Omar, and Bush)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 25 House supporters, all Democrats.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Mike Rogers (R-AL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 supporters were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-majority Armed Services Committee gave it no action [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill cuts $100 billion from authorized Pentagon funding, which would reduce contracts for weapons, operations, and research. Contractors benefit from the bill's death: their revenue stream was never put to a vote.

industries.industry: Military health care providers and Defense civilian workforce
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts the Defense Health Program and civil service pay and benefits, protecting military health care and civilian jobs from any reduction.
